newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president backs elections demand.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president backs elections demand.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president gave cheer to a national opposition protest movement by echoing its calls for early elections to help the country to escape from a political and economic quagmire.

Petar Stoyanov, a member of the opposition, won a warm welcome from anti-government protesters who took to the streets for a 14th day and more cautious one from the Socialist government of former communists.

"I am now convinced that the only alternative to end this terrible crisis is to make a change and that change is early parliamentary elections," he told a crowd after taking the oath of office on Sunday.
Cathedral bells rang and protesters danced or carried doves and snowdrops to symbolise hope, but details of any breakthrough in a political deadlock remained to be hammered out.

"I will begin immediate consultations with the political forces," said Stoyanov, who kept his options last week open by saying he might reluctantly grant the Socialists a new government mandate denied them by predecessor Zhelyu Zhelev.
The Socialist nominee to be new prime minister, Nikolai Dobrev, offered an ambiguous tribute to Stoyanov, of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) which is leading the protests.
"By nominating Petar Stoyanov as a president, the UDF has elected the best of itself," he said.
No let-up was likely on Monday in the demonstrations and symbolic strikes calling for speedy elections. Taxi drivers planned protest cavalcades in 12 provincial cities.
About 20,000 people turned out in Sofia on Sunday. Girls painted hearts their cheeks in the blue colour of the opposition and boys had the UDF initials across their faces.

"We have to listen to the young people in the streets as they are the power of the future and it is our duty to give them an incentive to stay, to work and to live in this country," Stoyanov said, referring to the many young Bulgarians who leave to seek a better life abroad.

He urged politicians of all parties to work together to introduce measures to bring the country out of crisis, including a tough IMF-backed fixed exchange rate regime, greater financial discipline and a crackdown on corruption.
Stoyanov, who formally takes office on Wednesday, said he was cancelling a celebration reception "as a show of solidarity with the impoverished population."
Bulgarian incomes are now worth only a few dollars a month, fuelling demands for elections not constitutionally required for nearly two years.
The Socialists have offered elections by the end of the year and a second Socialist cabinet in the meantime. The opposition objects to any new government led by the former communists.
"What they are suggesting is suicide, because it means delaying introduction of a currency board, delaying passing the budget and delaying talks with the IMF," said Dobrev.
Stoyanov was to meet business and industry chiefs on Monday to gather views on reforms likely to cause even more hardship in a state-run economy stricken with inflation of over 300 percent.
Meeting parliamentary leaders after his inauguration, he said any new government needed the support of all sides.

"We have to make the right choice, which is the European type of civilisation, to show our will and to build the conditions for our integration into the European Union and NATO," he said in his inaugural speech.
The government has dragged its feet on European and NATO integration, anxious not to alienate its old allies in Moscow.

Dobrev presented a short-term programme for his planned government to the Socialist leadership, including economic stabilisation measures like implementing a currency board mechanism, stabilising collapsing banks, improving tax revenue and closing loss-making state firms.
He denied planning to default on payments of Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
